Summary.1: Compared to peers operating in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra, which typically report sugar recovery rates of around 10%, our operations in Madhya Pradesh have consistently achieved a higher recovery rate of 11%.

This 1% improvement in yield directly enhances profitability, as it results in higher sugar output from the same quantity of sugarcane — thereby improving revenue without incurring any additional raw material or processing cost.
Since this incremental yield does not require any corresponding increase in input cost, it translates into pure margin expansion, improving both gross and EBITDA margins.
Over time, this operational efficiency becomes a key competitive advantage, especially in a cost-sensitive, commodity-driven industry like sugar.

While peers in the sugar industry typically report power generation as a separate revenue stream, Mahakaushal Sugar & Power Industries adopts a more conservative accounting approach by netting power income against operating costs.

Specifically, power generated through bagasse/corn-based cogeneration is primarily used for captive consumption, and the surplus exported to the grid is deducted from the cost of power/fuel instead of being reflected as top-line revenue.
This approach does not understate our profitability — rather, it provides a clearer reflection of net operational efficiency.
It also aligns with the principle of matching income directly with the cost it offsets, ensuring transparency in actual margin performance.

As a result, while our revenue figures may appear lower than peers due to this treatment, our reported margins remain fully comparable, and in fact, better reflect our cost savings from internal power generation.
While most leading sugar manufacturers have established their operations in states like Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, or Rajasthan.
But Mahakaushal Sugar & Power Ltd. has strategically chosen to situate its manufacturing plant in Madhya Pradesh.
(a region historically underserved in terms of large-scale sugar processing infrastructure.)
This decision appears to be driven by multiple strategic and operational advantages:
Significantly lower land acquisition and setup costs compared to UP and Maharashtra, enabling more cost-effective capital deployment.
A clear first-mover advantage in regions such as Mandla, Dindori, and Jabalpur, where sugarcane cultivation exists but had previously lacked local monetization avenues.
The absence of major competing sugar mills in the vicinity created an opportunity to serve a captive cane-producing farmer base, which would otherwise bear high transport costs to distant mills.
This allowed Mahakaushal to build deep-rooted supply chain relationships with local farmers, ensuring reliable raw material sourcing and enhancing long-term operational stability.
By entering an untapped geography with latent agricultural potential, the company has effectively positioned itself to optimize input costs, secure supply,
and contribute to rural economic development - while maintaining strong control over its value chain.
